title: A ‘light mill’ isn’t pushed by light: it spins the wrong way for that

cover.alt: A Crookes radiometer: a clear glass bulb on a glass stem, with small vanes inside, one black and one silvery, balanced on a needle.

body: William Crookes invented the radiometer in 1873: a glass bulb holding a partial vacuum, with vanes on a spindle that are black on one side and polished or white on the other. Put it in sunlight and it whirls, with the **black sides retreating** from the light. If the push of light itself were doing the work, it would turn the other way, and that push is far too weak to move the vanes anyway. What really happens is that the black sides warm up faster, and the thin gas left in the bulb creeps around the edges of each vane from the cool side to the warm side, building up pressure that shoves the cooler side forward.

slides.prompt: William Crookes, who invented the light mill in 1873, stumbled on its effect while doing ordinary lab work. What was he doing?
slides.answer: Weighing samples in a partial vacuum
slides.detail: He worked in a partly evacuated chamber to cut out air currents, and noticed that sunlight falling on his balance upset the weighings. Chasing that led him to the light mill.

left.label: Myth
left.text: Light hits the vanes and pushes them round.

right.label: Fact
right.text: Light’s push is far too small. Warm gas creeping round the vane edges does the work.

slides.heading: How a light mill really turns

steps.label: Light warms the black sides faster
Gas creeps round each edge, cold side to hot
Pressure builds behind the cooler white side
White side goes forward, black side trails

slides.label: the gas pressure at which the spin is strongest
slides.text: More gas inside holds the vanes back. By 0.0001 pascals the effect is gone, and in a hard vacuum the vanes stay still.

slides.heading: Who worked it out
slides.text: Osborne Reynolds proposed the accepted explanation, thermal transpiration: gas seeps from the cooler to the warmer side of a porous plate, and the edges of a vane act like those pores. His paper was refereed by James Clerk Maxwell, who published his own paper on the problem.

slides.heading: Which way does it spin?

items.text: Warmed up in a dark room

slides.explanation: Warming makes the black sides hotter, so it turns forward. Cooling the bulb quickly runs it backwards for a minute or two until it settles.
